items.title: Parsons Prepares for Next Week's Giving Tuesday
items.summary: Thirty-six local organizations are taking part in this year’s Giving Tuesday Match Day in Parsons. Parsons Area Community Foundation Becky Dantic, in an update to the Labette County Commission, says the foundation has awarded about $4.4 million in competitive grants since 1998. She says Giving Tuesday helps local organizations build a source of funding they can count on year after year . Dantic says past Match Days have raised about $1.7 million. The foundation’s 11th annual Giving Tuesday event runs from 7:00am to 7:00pm Tuesday, December 1st, at the Cardinal Event Center in Parsons.

items.title: Trump Halts Iowa Army Explosives Detonation as Toxic Lead Concerns, Federal Lawsuit and Decades-Old Warnings Converge
items.summary: Nearly five tons of deteriorating lead azide have placed the military, environmental regulators, and neighboring communities in a difficult position. A presidential directive has halted the planned operation pending court approval and agreement from Iowa's governor-elect, but newly examined records raise questions about how the emergency developed. By Miami News-Digest | Staff Report November 23, 2026 WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Monday that he has ordered the U.S. Army not to proceed with the planned detonation of nearly five tons of deteriorating explosive material at an Iowa ammunition plant unless a federal appeals court authorizes the operation and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand agrees to it. The announcement marks a significant reversal in a rapidly developing dispute that has placed military explosives specialists, environmental regulators, public health officials, and concerned residents on opposite sides of an extraordinary safety decision. At the center of the controversy are 68 drums containing approximately 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive compound used in military detonators. items.title: Guthrie’s Historic Homes Tour to Open Doors to Oklahoma’s Territorial Past Dec. 5
items.summary: GUTHRIE, Okla. — Nov. 23, 2026 — Visitors will have an opportunity to explore some of Oklahoma’s historic architecture during Guthrie’s Distinctive Homes Tour on Saturday, Dec. 5, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., including a stop at the Oklahoma Territorial Museum and Carnegie Library. The Oklahoma Historical Society announced Monday that the museum will participate in the annual holiday event, which highlights historic homes and landmark buildings in Guthrie, Oklahoma’s original state capital. The tour is part of Guthrie’s Territorial Christmas celebration, a longstanding seasonal tradition that combines architectural preservation, local history, and holiday festivities. Participating properties will feature Christmas decorations, while visitors can learn about the buildings and the people who occupied them during the city's early development. At the Carnegie Library, guests will be offered wassail, a traditional spiced holiday beverage. The historic library, constructed in 1902 with funding from philanthropist Andrew Carnegie, played an important role in Oklahoma's transition from territorial government to statehood. items.title: Calm Waters Offers Free Holiday Grief Workshop for Oklahoma Families
items.summary: OKLAHOMA CITY, Okla. — Nov. 23, 2026 — For families grieving the death of a loved one, the holiday season can bring difficult emotions alongside familiar traditions and celebrations. An Oklahoma nonprofit hopes to help children and adults find comfort, connection, and practical ways to cope. Calm Waters Center for Children and Families will host a free workshop, Coping with Grief Through the Holidays, on Thursday, Dec. 10, from 6 to 7:30 p.m. at its Oklahoma City facility. The program welcomes adults, teenagers, and children ages 3 and older who are navigating grief following the death of someone close to them. "The holidays can feel overwhelming when someone you love is missing," said Trisha Koelsch, chief executive officer of Calm Waters. The workshop is intended to provide a supportive environment where participants can discuss their experiences, preserve meaningful family traditions, and explore healthy ways to remember loved ones. Children will participate in age-appropriate activities, including a hands-on craft project honoring someone they have lost. items.title: USDA awards $5.4 million to fight feral hogs in Missouri as regional control efforts expand
items.summary: Federal funding also supports feral swine control in northeastern Oklahoma, including Ottawa and Delaware counties. MIAMI, Okla. — The U.S. Department of Agriculture has awarded approximately $5.4 million to three Missouri conservation projects aimed at eliminating invasive feral hogs, protecting agricultural lands, and reducing environmental damage across the Ozarks. The funding, announced Nov. 3, is part of a nationwide $51.9 million investment supporting 29 projects across 13 states through the USDA's Feral Swine Eradication and Control Pilot Program. The Missouri Department of Conservation will administer three federally funded projects, including $2,233,608 for the Ozark Highlands, $1,405,500 for the White River region, and $1,713,453 for the Missouri Lakes region. The projects will support trapping operations, landowner assistance, habitat restoration, and efforts to prevent the spread of feral swine into previously cleared areas. items.title: Students in southwest Missouri will help transform donated deer into meals for families facing food insecurity
items.summary: MARSHFIELD, Mo. — Students in southwest Missouri will help transform donated deer into meals for families facing food insecurity through a new conservation partnership, while the Cherokee Nation is expanding a similar venison donation program across its reservation in northeastern Oklahoma. The Missouri Department of Conservation announced Nov. 10 that Marshfield School District will host the state's first school-based Share the Harvest deer donation drive Dec. 5-6 in Webster County. The initiative brings together conservation officials, agricultural education students, local hunters, and Zimmerman Quality Meats to provide locally harvested venison to families in need. Hunters may donate legally harvested deer at Marshfield High School's Agriculture Building, 370 State Highway DD, from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. both days. All donated deer must be field-dressed and registered through Missouri's Telecheck system before drop-off. Zimmerman Quality Meats will process the donated animals for community distribution, including the school district's backpack food assistance program. Hunters will not be charged processing fees. items.title: Cherokee Nation to Invest in Weather Warning Upgrades
items.summary: The Cherokee Nation is investing more than $13 million to prepare for severe weather across northeast Oklahoma. The funding will be used to install or upgrade outdoor warning sirens and provide residential tornado shelters. Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Junior says the Cherokee Nation has a responsibility to prepare for emergencies before they happen. The Tribe received an eight-million-dollar FEMA grant for the project and will provide up to$2 million in additional tribal funding through the Public Health and Wellness Act. The project is aimed at helping Cherokee families better prepare for severe weather.

items.title: Kansas Sports Facilities Authority Holds First Meeting
items.summary: The Kansas Sports Facilities Authority has held its first meeting, taking several steps toward construction of the new Kansas City Chiefs stadium and facilities in Kansas. Lieutenant Governor and Commerce Secretary David Toland was elected chair of the authority. Toland says the meeting establishes the leadership and organizational structure needed to oversee the project. The eleven-member authority will oversee construction, financing and management of the sports facilities and related infrastructure. The project includes a three-billion-dollar fixed-roof stadium in Wyandotte County and a new Chiefs headquarters and practice facility in Johnson County. The facilities will be surrounded by planned mixed-use development, including potential sports, entertainment, dining, shopping, hotels and housing. The Chiefs are expected to begin playing in the new stadium in 2031. The authority also approved bylaws, legal counsel and a series of agreements covering construction, management, community impact and the team’s commitment to remain in Kansas.

items.title: BREAKING: FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop Following Air Traffic Control Communications Failure
items.summary: Flights halted across the United States Friday afternoon as federal aviation officials investigate widespread communications problems. MIAMI, Okla. — November 13, 2026 | Miami News-Digest The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, November 13, temporarily suspending aircraft departures across the United States after a widespread communications failure affected the nation's air traffic control system. The emergency directive was issued for aviation safety reasons as federal technicians investigated problems affecting all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which manage aircraft traveling between airports across the country. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the communications disruption and said FAA technicians were working to identify and resolve the problem. According to Reuters and the Associated Press, aircraft already airborne were permitted to continue flying and land at their destinations, while departing aircraft were instructed to remain on the ground. items.title: Bear Wrestling, $1 Swearing Fines, and Other Strange Oklahoma Laws Still on the Books
items.summary: From fortune-telling and cemetery bird eggs to Sunday car sales, Oklahoma's legal history contains some surprisingly unusual provisions. MIAMI, Okla. — Oklahoma is a state known for its colorful history, independent spirit, and occasionally peculiar traditions. However, some of its strangest stories are not found in museums, folklore, or dusty history books. They are written into the state's laws. Buried within the Oklahoma Statutes are provisions addressing everything from wrestling bears and charging for psychic readings to using religious names in casual conversation. items.summary: Judicial compensation proposal carried an estimated $10 million price tag, while court-reporter shortages and questions about transparency continue to confront the state. By Miami News-Digest | November 5, 2026 OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma judges sought substantial salary increases through the state's judicial compensation process, but lawmakers rejected a proposed 17.58% raise earlier this year, bringing renewed attention to the competing demands of judicial compensation, taxpayer spending, and the performance of the state's court system. The Oklahoma Board on Judicial Compensation recommended the increase on September 16, 2025, citing comparatively low judicial salaries and the need to attract qualified candidates. Under the proposal, the Oklahoma Supreme Court chief justice's annual salary would have increased from $198,212 to approximately $233,062, while district judges would have received approximately $197,189, compared with their existing $167,703 salaries. Cleveland County District Judge Thad Balkman, then president of the Oklahoma Judges Association, estimated the proposal would cost approximately $10 million annually, covering 277 trial and appellate judges statewide. items.summary: A Sacred Legacy: Historic Quapaw Crucifix Preserves More Than a Century of Native American Catholic Heritage in Miami From a 19th-century mission on Quapaw land to Sacred Heart Catholic Church, a remarkable crucifix tells a story of faith, tribal leadership, sacrifice, and remembrance. By Miami News-Digest MIAMI, Okla. — Behind glass at Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Miami rests a remarkable piece of northeastern Oklahoma history: a wooden crucifix connected to St. Mary's of the Quapaws, a Catholic mission established in Indian Territory more than 130 years ago. Mounted against a dark blue background, the crucifix bears a small inscription identifying its origins: "Crucifix from St. Mary of the Quapaws, 1893–1927." Yet the religious artifact represents considerably more than the history of a church. It preserves a connection between generations of Quapaw families, the early development of Catholicism in northeastern Oklahoma, and a mission whose legacy extended far beyond its closing nearly a century ago. items.summary: Oklahoma Supreme Court Blocks Property-Tax Phaseout in Narrow 5-4 Decision Majority says State Question 843 conflicted with Oklahoma Constitution; dissenters question whether courts should stop citizen initiatives before voters act By Miami News-Digest OKLAHOMA CITY — A divided Oklahoma Supreme Court has stopped an initiative that sought to phase out most property taxes on owner-occupied homes, ruling 5-4 that the proposal directly conflicted with Oklahoma’s Constitution before supporters could begin gathering signatures to place it before voters. The court issued its decision Monday, Oct. 5, in Brooks v. Reynolds, 2026 OK 71, declaring State Question 843, Initiative Petition 455, “clearly and manifestly” unconstitutional. The decision presents two distinct questions that divided the court: whether the proposed tax exemption conflicted with existing constitutional rules governing property taxation, and whether the Supreme Court should decide such a constitutional question before an initiative has been enacted by voters at all.
